coach_says: Your knight on d4 was attacked by the c6 knight and only your queen on d1 guarded it. Bd3 stands right on the d-file between them, so the queen no longer protects d4 and Black simply plays ...Nxd4 and wins a piece. Before developing a piece, ask whether it blocks a defender; here Nxc6 first (or f3/Be3) kept everything protected.
concept: blocked the queen's defence of d4

coach_says: Your c-pawn was strong on c3: Rc5 would have attacked the knight and protected the pawn, and if Nxc3 then Rxc3 wins the knight. After c2 Rc1 the pawn is stuck on a square White can blockade, your rook gets tied to defending it, and White's king and knight can come over to pick it up. In an endgame, keep your passed pawn supported and use your rook actively, rather than pushing it to a square where it can be blockaded and won.
concept: pushed the passer into a blockade

coach_says: White's knight on f3 was already attacking your e5 pawn, and Bc5 does nothing to guard it, so Nxe5 just wins a pawn. Before developing, check whether the opponent's last move created a threat. Nc6 defends e5 and develops at the same time; Bc5 can come next move.

White's king is still on e1 with no f-pawn or g-pawn in front of it, and his pieces are undeveloped. Qh4+ hits it straight away: the king can't castle and has to walk forward to d2 or e2, where your knights and bishop can join the attack. b5 just defends a pawn and gives White time to tidy up. When the enemy king is exposed, look at checks and direct attacks before slow pawn moves.

Your rook on d3 was attacked by the king, but it could take something before leaving: Rxd2+ gives the rook for the bishop with check, and then Rxc6 wins the c6 bishop, which nothing defends. Retreating with Rdd8 lets White save the bishop with Bb5 and keep the extra piece. When one of your pieces is attacked, first ask whether it can capture something on its way out.

Your knight had to move away from ...cxd3, and the question was where it does the most. On c5 it gets kicked at once by ...b6 and has to go to the edge on a6. Ne5 sits in the centre, attacks the loose c4 pawn and teams up with your rook on e7 against f7, so Black can't hold everything. When you move a knight, check whether a pawn can chase it away from its new square.

Your bishop was attacked by d5, but Bd3 is a passive retreat that blocks your own d-pawn and your c1 bishop. Re1+ first uses the open e-file with check, then Bb5 pins the c6 knight and keeps the bishop active, and you can play d4 freely. When a piece is attacked, look for a retreat that gains time or does a job, not just a safe square.

After Bxe5 fxe5, White's pawn arrives with an attack on your f6 knight. That knight is guarding d5, which the b3 bishop and d1 rook both attack, so it can't move without dropping the d5 knight. Before trading, look at what the recapture attacks. Rad8 adds a defender to d5 and keeps your good position.
also: pressure on the pinned d5 knight

coach_says: Your knight on g5 was attacked by h6, and Bh7+ does not solve that. After Kh8 the bishop has to go back to d3, the knight is still attacked, and Black plays ...Nb4 or ...Ne5 to swap off your bishop while you finally retreat the knight. A check that has to be undone costs you time; here the simple Nf3 was best.

Good move. Your b1 bishop was attacked by the rook, and instead of saving it you hit White's c4 bishop with d5, so after Rxb1 dxc4 you win a piece back. Answering a threat with a counter-threat is a useful idea to keep in mind.
Nc6 is about as good as anything here; the engine's top moves are all close. Your position was already difficult and this move develops a piece toward d4. Nothing specific to fix on this move.
Be2 is a fine move, very close to the engine's choice. It removes the bishop from the d-file so your rook can take the d4 pawn. Bc4 was a touch more active, but the difference is small.
Kd3 brings your king toward the action and keeps you winning comfortably. Using the bishop first to collect the f4 pawn was slightly cleaner, but the difference is tiny.

Black's knight on e5 was already attacking your c4 bishop, and f4 ignores that: Black just takes it with ...Nxc4 and you lose your pair of bishops. Your bishops are your trump against Black's extra pawns, so keep them. Bb3 saves the bishop, and you can still kick the knight with f4 later.
also: kicking a piece that can capture first

coach_says: Rd1 does guard the d2 bishop, but it leaves your b5 knight and c6 bishop loose. ...Rb6 attacks both at once and you have to give material back. Nd4 was the move: it blocks the d-file so the bishop on d2 is safe, and it defends c6. When you see one threat, check that your answer doesn't leave other pieces unprotected.
concept: loose pieces hit by a rook fork

coach_says: f4 hits the queen, but it opens the long diagonal: Qe4 attacks your rook on a8 and, together with the c2 bishop, threatens Qxh7+. You have to block with ...Nf6 and the f4 pawn falls. Nc6 was better, because it protects your queen on e7, so the e6 pawn can recapture on f5 without losing the queen. Before chasing the queen, check where it can go and what it hits from there.
also: queen and bishop aimed at h7

coach_says: Your e5 pawn was attacked by both the d4 pawn and the f3 knight, and d5 doesn't defend it, so Nxe5 just wins a pawn. ...e4 kicking the knight or ...exd4 were the moves that dealt with it. When a pawn is attacked, protect it, move it or trade it before playing anything else.

Black's bishop on g4 had just taken your knight and was attacking your queen on d1. Bxd6 trades bishops but leaves the queen to be taken: ...Bxd1. Qxg4 recaptures and keeps the material level. When the opponent captures, first ask what that piece now attacks, especially your queen.

White's queen on e4 and bishop on c2 were both aiming at h7, so Qxh7+ was already threatened, and Nb6 does nothing about it. After Qxh7+ Kf7 Qh5+ Kg8 Bh7+ Kh8 Bg6+ Kg8 Qh7 it's mate. Nf6 blocks the diagonal and attacks the queen at the same time. Each move, check what your opponent's queen and bishop line up on.
concept: missed the mate threat on h7

coach_says: Black has pushed ...g5 and ...h6, which loosens his kingside. f4 hits the g5 pawn at once and opens the f-file for your rook. Qf3 blocks your own f-pawn and lets ...Ne5 attack the queen with tempo, so your advantage disappears. When the opponent overextends his pawns, look for the pawn break that attacks them.
